# ducknng transport adapters and carrier boundaries

This document defines the transport-family boundary for `ducknng`. It is intentionally narrower than `docs/protocol.md`: the protocol document defines the manifest methods, session lifecycle, and payload rules, while this document defines how those same contracts are carried over concrete transport adapters.

The core rule is simple. Transport adapters may change how bytes move, but they do not change what the bytes mean. The `ducknng` envelope remains the method layer, Arrow IPC remains the tabular payload layer, JSON remains the control-metadata layer, and the manifest remains the source of truth for public RPC methods. A new transport adapter is therefore not a license to mint parallel method names or alternate session semantics.

Today `ducknng` has two implemented transport families. The NNG family covers `inproc://`, `ipc://`, `tcp://`, `tls+tcp://`, `ws://`, and `wss://`, all of which resolve into the NNG adapter layer isolated in `src/ducknng_nng_compat.c`. The HTTP family covers `http://` and `https://` through the separate adapter in `src/ducknng_http_compat.c`, built on NNG's supplemental HTTP APIs rather than on NNG protocol sockets. The transport-family parser that classifies URL schemes lives separately in `src/ducknng_transport.c` so the SQL layer can pick one family cleanly before handing control to the appropriate adapter.

The stable scheme matrix is:

| Surface | Accepted schemes | TLS handle accepted on | Explicitly rejected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ducknng_start_server(...)` | `inproc://`, `ipc://`, `tcp://`, `tls+tcp://`, `ws://`, `wss://`, `http://`, `https://` | `tls+tcp://`, `wss://`, `https://` | unknown schemes; TLS handles on non-TLS schemes |
| generic socket API (`ducknng_dial_socket`, `ducknng_listen_socket`) | `inproc://`, `ipc://`, `tcp://`, `tls+tcp://`, `ws://`, `wss://` | `tls+tcp://`, `wss://` | `http://`, `https://` |
| synchronous RPC/session helpers (`ducknng_request`, `ducknng_get_rpc_manifest`, `ducknng_run_rpc`, `ducknng_query_rpc`, `ducknng_open_query`, `ducknng_fetch_query`, `ducknng_fetch_query_table`, `ducknng_close_query`, `ducknng_cancel_query`) | NNG schemes plus `http://`, `https://` | `tls+tcp://`, `wss://`, `https://` | unknown schemes; TLS handles on non-TLS schemes |
| synchronous raw RPC/session helpers (`ducknng_get_rpc_manifest_raw`, `ducknng_run_rpc_raw`, `ducknng_open_query_raw`, `ducknng_fetch_query_raw`, `ducknng_close_query_raw`, `ducknng_cancel_query_raw`, `ducknng_request_raw`) | NNG schemes plus `http://`, `https://` | `tls+tcp://`, `wss://`, `https://` | unknown schemes; TLS handles on non-TLS schemes |
| raw RPC/session AIO helpers (`ducknng_request_raw_aio`, `ducknng_get_rpc_manifest_raw_aio`, `ducknng_run_rpc_raw_aio`, `ducknng_open_query_raw_aio`, `ducknng_fetch_query_raw_aio`, `ducknng_close_query_raw_aio`, `ducknng_cancel_query_raw_aio`) | NNG schemes plus `http://`, `https://` | `tls+tcp://`, `wss://`, `https://` | unknown schemes; TLS handles on non-TLS schemes |
| HTTP client helpers (`ducknng_ncurl`, `ducknng_ncurl_aio`, `ducknng_ncurl_table`) | `http://`, `https://` | `https://` | NNG schemes, unknown schemes, TLS handles on `http://` |

`tls_config_id = 0` means no TLS handle. Supplying a non-zero TLS handle on a non-TLS URL is rejected rather than silently ignored. This is part of the security contract: if an operator supplied TLS material, the connection must either use a TLS-capable scheme or fail before dialing/listening.

The generic socket API reports expected failures in-band. Its synchronous helpers return a struct with `ok`, `error`, nullable `nng_error`, nullable `nng_error_message`, `socket_id`, `payload`, and `url`. NNG-returned failures use the numeric NNG error and `nng_strerror()` text; ducknng validation failures, such as trying to dial `https://` through the NNG socket layer, keep those NNG fields NULL.

HTTP is not just a spelling of NNG `tcp://`, and HTTPS is not just a spelling of NNG `tls+tcp://`. They share lower network layers, but their application framing is different. NNG `tcp://` and `tls+tcp://` carry NNG scalability-protocol frames directly over streams. HTTP/HTTPS carries HTTP requests and responses with methods, paths, headers, status codes, and bodies; `ducknng` places exactly one framed RPC envelope in that HTTP body. Likewise, NNG `ws://` and `wss://` use an HTTP/WebSocket handshake but then carry the NNG WebSocket mapping for scalability protocols, so they remain in the NNG family rather than becoming HTTP carrier routes.

The HTTP and HTTPS family surfaces through the same primary server helper as the NNG family: `ducknng_start_server(...)` chooses the carrier from the URL scheme, and `http://` / `https://` listeners must use `contexts = 1` because the HTTP carrier does not expose the NNG REP-context model. `ducknng_ncurl(...)` and `ducknng_ncurl_aio(...)` remain the low-level HTTP transport primitives; when supplied with a registered outbound HTTP profile id, they resolve credentials inside the HTTP client path after fail-closed scope checks rather than requiring caller SQL to pass secret headers. SQL scalar helpers that start or stop services, mutate service policy, or perform synchronous transport/RPC/session I/O are registered `VOLATILE`; DuckDB must not fold them as constants or reuse their results across recursive or repeated execution. Deterministic frame and body inspection helpers may remain `CONSISTENT`. Table-function carriers do not currently have a C API volatility flag, so dynamic-schema helpers such as `ducknng_ncurl_table(...)` are not the right primitive for per-row retry or fanout plans; use volatile raw scalars such as `ducknng_ncurl(...)` plus explicit parsing when repeated execution matters. The route helpers `ducknng_register_http_route(...)`, `ducknng_register_http_route_pattern(...)`, `ducknng_unregister_http_route(...)`, `ducknng_unregister_http_route_pattern(...)`, `ducknng_list_http_routes()`, `ducknng_http_request()`, and `ducknng_http_request_body()` are also transport-local HTTP helpers, not new manifest methods. The manifest does not gain `http_exec`, `http_query_open`, `http_fetch`, or similar duplicates. It continues to describe `manifest`, `exec`, `query_open`, `fetch`, `close`, and `cancel` once, independent of whether the current carrier is NNG or HTTP. The concrete HTTP contracts are pinned in `docs/http.md` for the framed carrier and `docs/http_server_framework.md` for the companion route layer. When route SQL needs per-request dynamic session control, the raw synchronous session helpers plus the low-level frame scalar accessors (`ducknng_frame_version(...)`, `ducknng_frame_type(...)`, `ducknng_frame_flags(...)`, `ducknng_frame_type_name(...)`, `ducknng_frame_name(...)`, `ducknng_frame_payload(...)`, `ducknng_frame_payload_text(...)`, `ducknng_frame_error_text(...)`, and `ducknng_frame_end_of_stream(...)`) are the route-safe surface; the structured table helpers remain the ergonomic client surface.

This matters most for sessions, authentication, and execution policy. Under the HTTP transport adapter, `query_open` still accepts the same one-row Arrow IPC control payload with `sql` and optional batch hints, and returns the same `session_id`, `session_token`, and server-owned effective `idle_timeout_ms` control metadata. `fetch` still accepts JSON control metadata keyed by `session_id` and `session_token`. `fetch` still returns either Arrow IPC row batches or JSON control metadata. `close` and `cancel` still consume JSON control payloads and still return JSON control replies. The session state machine is unchanged. Only the outer carrier changes. Existing synchronous request, RPC, and session helpers route by URL scheme so HTTP remains a carrier under the same operation-oriented API instead of becoming a second RPC client surface. The same is true for the current DuckDB execution contract: `server.execution.model` and the matching `ducknng_list_servers().execution_model` value are carrier-neutral service metadata, not transport-specific branches. When `tls+tcp://`, `wss://`, or `https://` is configured for required peer authentication, the same verified mTLS caller identity is attached to the request context and used for session ownership regardless of carrier. Service peer and IP/CIDR allowlists are also carrier-neutral at the policy level: NNG transports enforce the fast C path with `nng_pipe_notify(..., NNG_PIPE_EV_ADD_PRE, ...)`, verified TLS pipe metadata, `NNG_OPT_REMADDR`, and dispatch re-checks, while HTTP/HTTPS checks the corresponding connection metadata and returns HTTP `403` before RPC dispatch. NNG services also record `ADD_PRE`, `ADD_POST`, and `REM_POST` pipe events in a bounded monitor stream readable with `ducknng_read_monitor(...)`, including denial reasons when available from the fast C admission path. They expose ring/counter metadata with `ducknng_monitor_status(...)` and maintain an active-pipe snapshot readable with `ducknng_list_pipes(...)`; these are transport telemetry and application-event foundations, not a new wire protocol. `docs/mesh_routing_demo.md` sketches how those primitives can be composed into a future routing demo without sealing a router API. The flexible SQL authorizer is likewise carrier-neutral at the request boundary: `ducknng_auth_context()` exposes the same core columns for NNG and HTTP/HTTPS framed RPC, with HTTP-only columns such as method, path, and content type populated when available.

The same rule holds for Arrow record batches. The HTTP adapter does not reinterpret row batches as ad hoc JSON arrays or text serialization just because the outer transport is HTTP. When a method returns Arrow IPC over NNG, it returns Arrow IPC over HTTP. When a method returns JSON control metadata over NNG, it returns JSON control metadata over HTTP. Content headers may help a client understand the body, but they do not replace the method contract.

The intended code boundary is therefore three-way. Transport-family parsing belongs in transport-neutral code such as `ducknng_transport.c`. NNG-specific socket, listener, TLS, peer-identity extraction from NNG pipes, and aio details belong in `ducknng_nng_compat.c`. HTTP-specific client/server details and peer-identity extraction from HTTP connections belong in `ducknng_http_compat.c`. The SQL layer should choose a transport family once from the URL scheme and then hand off to the appropriate adapter instead of scattering scheme-specific branches through session, wire, or Arrow code.

Because this transport-family split is explicit, `http://` and `https://` URLs are rejected by the generic NNG socket layer rather than being silently passed into NNG operations. At the same time, the synchronous request, RPC, and session helpers now route over those schemes through the HTTP adapter, while `ducknng_ncurl(...)` and `ducknng_ncurl_aio(...)` remain the low-level HTTP/HTTPS transport primitives. `ws://` and `wss://` stay on the NNG side of the boundary: they are NNG transports, not aliases for the HTTP carrier.
